units.la: Hæc imitatio ad honorem sanctorum vel maximè pertinet, ut ad Philip. 2. scriptum est: Sitis irreprehensibiles in medio nationis pravæ, inter quos lucete, tanquam luminaria in mundo, ad gloriam meam in die Christi. Et 1. Thess. 2. Vos estis gloria nostra & corona gloriationis nostræ. Passim etiam alibi hanc imitationem præcipit Scriptura, ut Heb. 6. Ne sitis segnes, sed imitatores eorum, qui per fidem & per patientiam hereditatem acceperunt promissionum. Et Hebr. 13. Quorum intuentes exitum conversationis, imitemini fidem. Et Phil. 3. & 1. Thess. 1, Imitatores nostri estis, & observate eos, qui ita ita ambulant, sicut nos habetis pro exemplari. Quò pertinent etiam hæc dicta Augustini & Chrysostomi. Sic enim Augustinus de verâ religione cap. 55. inquit: Sancti honorandi sunt propter imitationem, non adorandi propter religionem. Chrysostomus verò: Non est justitia, sanctos colere, & sanctitatem contemnere. Primus ad sanctitatem gradus est, sanctitatem diligere.
units.tr: This imitation pertains above all to the honour of the saints, as is written in Philippians 2: Be blameless in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine as lights in the world, to my glory on the day of Christ. And 1 Thessalonians 2: You are our glory and the crown of our rejoicing. Scripture commands this imitation everywhere else too, as in Hebrews 6: Be not slothful, but imitators of those who through faith and patience inherited the promises. And Hebrews 13: Considering the outcome of their conduct, imitate their faith. And Philippians 3 and 1 Thessalonians 1: Be imitators of us, and observe those who walk thus, as you have us as an example. To this belong also the sayings of Augustine and Chrysostom. For Augustine in his book On True Religion, chapter 55, says: The saints are to be honoured for the sake of imitation, not adored for the sake of religion. Chrysostom says: It is not justice to cultivate the saints and despise holiness. The first step to holiness is to love holiness.

units.la: ALIUD JESUITARUM SOPHISMA.
units.tr: ANOTHER SOPHISM OF THE JESUITS.

units.la: Etiam Augustinus non modò contra Faustum, sed etiam in libris de civitate Dei, discernit inter λατρείαν & δουλείαν.
units.tr: Augustine too, not only against Faustus but also in the books On the City of God, distinguishes between latreia [λατρείαν] and douleia [δουλείαν].

units.la: Ergo secundum Augustini quoq; sententiam nihil detrahitur de gloria Dei per sanctorum invocationem, si addatur hæc cautio: ut summus honos, summus cultus, qui λατρεία dicitur, summo Deo & mediatori Christo debitus, integrè conservetur.
units.tr: Therefore, according to Augustine's opinion too, nothing is taken away from the glory of God through the invocation of saints, provided this caution is added: that the highest honour and the highest worship, which is called latreia, due to the highest God and to Christ the Mediator, be kept entire.

units.la: Resp. Simpliciter hæc contradictoria sunt: Tribuere invocationem ulli creaturæ; & integrè conservare velle summum honorem, summumque cultum, qui λατρεία dicitur, summo Deo & mediatori Christo debitum. Nam invocatio est hic ipse summus honos, summusque cultus, sive λατρεία, quæ uni atque soli Deo, & mediatori Christo debetur: juxta hęc dicta. Psal. 50. Invoca me in die tribulationis. lationis. Et Joel. 2. Rom. 10. Omnis qui invocaverit nomen Domini, salvus erit. Item 1. Cor. 1. Gratia & pax sit omnib. qui invocant nomen Domini nostri Jesu Christi. 2. Tim. 2. Et discedat ab iniquitate omnis, qui invocat nomen Domini.
units.tr: Reply. These things are simply contradictory: to attribute invocation to any creature, and yet to wish to keep entire the highest honour and highest worship, which is called latreia, due to the highest God and to Christ the Mediator. For invocation is itself that highest honour and highest worship, or latreia, which is owed to the one and only God and to Christ the Mediator, according to these words: Psalm 50, Call upon me in the day of trouble. And Joel 2; Romans 10, Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved. Likewise 1 Corinthians 1, Grace and peace be to all who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. 2 Timothy 2, And let everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord depart from iniquity.

units.la: Idem & definitio λατρείας demonstrat. Nam summus cultus, qui λατρεία dicitur, est agnoscere, eum, quem invocamus, omnium pectorum motus videre: & certò atq; indubitatò credere, quòd & velit & possit in omni necessitate nobis succurrere, & bona animæ & corporis largiri. Quod non est, nisi immensæ atq; infinitę tùm omniscientiæ, tum omnipotentiæ, tùm etiam bonitatis Dei. Itaq; tribuere invocationem sive angelis, sive hominibus, est illis λατρείαν & honorem proprium divinitatis tribuere. Nihil igitur loci relinquum est cautioni illi minimè cautæ, de sic invocandis Sanctis, ut λατρείας conservetur, quo & Mediatori Christo debita.
units.tr: The definition of latreia shows the same thing. For the highest worship, which is called latreia, is to acknowledge that the one whom we invoke sees the movements of all hearts, and to believe with certainty and without doubt that he both is willing and able to come to our aid in every need, and to bestow the goods of soul and body. This cannot be so unless God has immeasurable and infinite omniscience, omnipotence and goodness. Therefore to attribute invocation to angels or to men is to attribute to them latreia, and the honour proper to divinity. Nothing therefore remains of room for that caution, which is in no way cautious, that saints be invoked in such a way that the latreia which is owed also to Christ the Mediator be preserved.

units.la: Præterea summa injuria fit Augustino, cùm Jesuitæ ad invocationem Sanctorum detorquent, quæ ille nequaquam de invocatione (quæ gradus nullos recipit, sed in universum atque omnino est cultus ille summus, unicè Deo & Mediatori debitus) sed in genere de vocabulo cultus (scripsit, cujus gradus distinctos facit, λατρείαν & δουλείαν. Quod ut evidentissimè appareat, verba ipsa Augustini optimâ fide recensebo. Sic igitur contra Faustum:
units.tr: Moreover, great injustice is done to Augustine when the Jesuits twist to the invocation of saints things which he never wrote about invocation (which admits of no degrees, but is that highest worship altogether and wholly due to God alone and the Mediator), but wrote about the general term cultus, whose distinct degrees he makes: latreia and douleia. So that this may appear most evidently, I shall set out Augustine's own words in good faith. Thus, then, against Faustus:

units.la: { } Augustinus ponit gradus invocationis & λατρείας: Sed cultus & honoris in genere. stum; cùm, ut supra citavimus, dixisset: Colimus Martyres eo cultu dilectionis, & societatis, quo & in hac vita coluntur sancti Dei homines. Mox addit: At illo cultu, qui Græcè λατρεία dicitur: Latinè uno verbo dici non potest; (cùm sit quadam proprie divinitati debita servitus) nec colimus, nec colendum docemus, nisi unum Deum. Cùm autem ad hunc cultum pertineat obla-tio sacrificii (unde Idololatria dicitur eorū, qui hoc etiam idolis exhibent) nullo modo talé aliquid offerimus, aut offerendum præcipimus, velcuiquam martyri, vel cuiquam sanctæ animæ, vel cuiquā angelo. Et quisquis in hunc errorem dilabitur, corripitur per sanam doctrinam, sive ut corrigatur, sive ut caveatur. Ipsi enim Sancti vel homines, vel angeli, exhiberi, sibi nolunt, quod uni Deo debeti norunt. Appparuit hoc in Paulo & Barnaba, Actor.14. cùm commoti miraculis, quæ per eos facta sunt, Lycaonii tanquam Diis immolare voluerunt. Conscijsis enim vestibus suis confitentes & persuadentes, se Deos non esse, ista sibi fieri vetuerunt. Apparuit & in Angelis, sicut in Apocalypsi legimus cap.19. Angelum se adorari prohibentem, ac dicentem adoratori suo: Conservus tuus sum, & fratrum tuorum.
units.tr: { } Augustine lays down degrees of invocation and of latreia; but he speaks of cultus and honour in general. ...when, as we cited above, he had said: We worship the martyrs with that worship of affection and fellowship with which the holy men of God are also worshipped in this life. Soon he adds: But with that worship which in Greek is called latreia, which cannot be expressed in Latin by one word (since it is a certain servitude due to divinity alone), we neither worship nor teach that anything is to be worshipped except the one God. Since the offering of sacrifice belongs to this worship (whence those who offer this also to idols are called idolaters), we in no way offer, or command to be offered, any such thing either to any martyr, or to any holy soul, or to any angel. And whoever slips into this error is rebuked through sound doctrine, either so that he may be corrected or so that he may be on his guard. For the holy men themselves, or the angels, do not wish to be given what they know is due to God alone. This appeared in Paul and Barnabas, Acts 14, when the Lycaonians, moved by the miracles done through them, wanted to sacrifice to them as to gods. For, tearing their garments, confessing and persuading, they forbade these things to be done to them, saying that they were not gods. It appeared also in the angels, as we read in Revelation 19, where an angel forbids himself to be worshipped and says to his worshipper: I am your fellow servant and of your brothers.

units.la: Ista sibi plane superbi spiritus exigunt, Diabolus & angeli ejus: sicut per omnia templa & sacra gentilium, quorum similitudo in quibusdam etiam superbis hominibus expressa est. Sicut de Babylonia quibusdam regibus memoria cum mendatum tenemus. Unde Sanctus Daniel accusatores & persecutores pertulit, quòd (regis edicto proposito, ut nihil à quoquam Deo peteretur, nisi à rege solùm) Deum suum, hoc est, unum & verum Deum adorare, deprecari, deprehensus est.
units.tr: These things are plainly demanded by proud spirits, the devil and his angels, as through all the temples and sacred rites of the Gentiles, whose likeness is expressed also in certain proud men. As we hold a memory, not false, of certain kings of Babylon. Whence Saint Daniel endured accusers and persecutors, because, when the king's edict had been published that nothing should be asked of any God except of the king alone, he was caught adoring and praying to his God, that is, the one and true God.

units.la: Hæc Augustinus lib. 2o. contra Faustum cap. 21. non stabiliens, sed efficacissimè refutans sophisma Jesuiticum. Quid potest enim dici clarius? quid evidentius? quàm quòd oblationem sacrificii (quæ est ipsa invocatio, & gratiarum actio) diserte ait pertinere ad λατρείαν uni Deo debitam? Et quòd expressa negat, vel cuiquam Martyri, vel cuiquam animæ sanctæ, vel cuiquam Angelo tale aliquid offerendum esse? Imò, quòd προσκύνησιν ait, ipsos sanctos exhiberi sibi nolle, quòd uni Deo debeatur: & quid hoc sit, exemplis declarat, non modò de immolatione, quam Paulus & Barnabas sibi fieri vetuerunt, sed etiam de adoratione, quæ est ipsa invocatio, quam Angelus adoratori suo prohibuerit? Deniq; quòd nominatim Diabolo & superbis hominibus afferibit, quòd se adorari, & à se peti postulaverint, cùm unum & verum Deū adorare ac deprecari liceat. Quòd si locum haberat commentitia illa distinctio graduum invocationis, qua Jesuitæ utuntur: cur non dixit Augustinus, oblationem sacrificii
units.tr: Augustine says these things in book 2 Against Faustus, chapter 21, not establishing but most effectively refuting the Jesuit sophism. What can be said more clearly? What more evident? than that he expressly says the offering of sacrifice (which is itself invocation and thanksgiving) pertains to the latreia due to the one God? And that he expressly denies that any such thing is to be offered to any martyr, or any holy soul, or any angel? Indeed, that he says the saints themselves do not wish to be shown proskynesis [προσκύνησιν], which is due to the one God; and he explains by examples what this is, not only about the immolation which Paul and Barnabas forbade to be made to themselves, but also about the adoration, which is invocation itself, which the angel forbade to his worshipper? Finally, that he attributes by name to the devil and to proud men that they demanded to be worshipped and asked of, when it is permitted to adore and pray to the one and true God. But if that fabricated distinction of degrees of invocation, which the Jesuits use, had any place, why did Augustine not say that the offering of sacrifice

units.la: I. II. III. (marginal numerals) ficii inferiori gradu competere etiam martyribus, aut animabus Sanctorum, aut Angelis? cur Paulus & Barnabas non inferiori gradu sibi immolari? cur non Angeli adorari fe gradu inferiori admiserunt? cur non eadem excusatione tueri fe reges Babyloniæ potuerunt? cur denique Daniel indiscrimen vitæ fe conjecit, non adhibita distinctione Jesuitica graduum invocationis?
units.tr: in a lower degree belongs also to martyrs, or to the souls of saints, or to angels? Why did Paul and Barnabas not allow themselves to be sacrificed to in a lower degree? Why did the angels not admit adoration in a lower degree? Why could the kings of Babylon not defend themselves by the same excuse? Why, finally, did Daniel cast himself into danger of his life, without applying the Jesuit distinction of degrees of invocation?

units.la: Jam lib. 10. de civitate Dei cap. 1. & alliquot sequentibus, distinctionem quidem λατρείας & δουλείας Augustinus inculcat, ut honorem & cultum, qui soli Deo debetur, discernat ab honore & cultu, qui creaturis etiam recte impenditur. (Vidit enim Scripturam docere, ut Deum diligamus, timeamus, honoremus, colamus, & ipsi serviamus. Eandem Scriptura præcipere, ut parentes honoremus, Dominis serviamus, amicos colamus, proximum diligamus, regé timeamus.) Sed nequaquam inter hæc (quæ præter Deum, hominibus etiam præstari possint inferiori aliquo gradu) invocationem & fiduciam cordis numerat. Imo vero, cum cultus, qui soli Deo tribuitur (ut est invocatio) transfertur ad creaturas, aperte idololatriam committit. Hic est enim status disputationis, quam tractat in eo libro Augustinus: utrum Angelis (quos Platonici Dæmonas vocant) placeat, ut etiam sibi, an tantum Deo suo, qui etiam noster est, sacra faciamus, vel aliqua nostra, seu nos ipsos religionis ritibus con-secremus? Et hic est, inquit, divinitati, vel si expressius dicendum est, Deitati debitus cultus, propter quem uno verbo significandum, quoniam satis idoneum non occurrit Latinum, Graece, ubi necesse est, insinuo, quid velim dicere. Λατρεία quippe nostri, ubicunque sanctarum scripturarum positum est, interpretatur servitutem. Sed ea servitus, qua debetur hominibus, secundum quam praecipit Apostolus, servos dominis suis subditos esse debere, alio nomine Graece nuncupari solet. Δουλεία vero secundum consuetudinem (qua locuti sunt, qui nobis divina eloquia condiderunt) aut semper, aut tam frequenter, ut pene semper ea dicitur servitus, quae pertinet ad colendum Deum. Proinde si tantummodo cultus ipse dicatur, (sc. in genere) non soli Deo deberi videtur. Dicimur enim etiam colere homines, quos honorifica vel recordatione, vel praesentia frequentamus: nec solum ea, quibus nos religiosa humilitate subjicimus; sed quaedam etiam, quae subjecta sunt nobis, coli perhibentur. Nam ex hoc verbo Agricola & Coloni & Incola vocantur. Et postea: Quia & aliarum rerum dicitur cultus, ideo latine uno verbo significari cultus Deo debitus non potest.
units.tr: Now in book 10 of the City of God, chapter 1 and some following, Augustine indeed insists on the distinction between latreia [λατρείας] and douleia [δουλείας], so that he may separate the honour and worship which is due to God alone from the honour and worship which is rightly paid also to creatures. (For he saw that Scripture teaches us to love, fear, honour and worship God, and to serve him. The same Scripture commands us to honour parents, serve masters, cultivate friends, love our neighbour, and fear the king.) But he by no means counts invocation and trust of heart among these things (which can be rendered to men also, apart from God, in some lower degree). Indeed, when the worship which is given to God alone (as invocation is) is transferred to creatures, he openly commits idolatry. For this is the state of the question which Augustine treats in that book: whether it pleases the angels (whom the Platonists call demons) that we perform sacred rites to them as to our own God, who is also ours, or whether we should consecrate some of our things, or ourselves, by rites of religion. And this, he says, is the worship due to divinity, or, if it must be said more expressly, to Deity; for which, since no Latin word suitably occurs to signify it in one word, I point out in Greek, where necessary, what I wish to say. For latreia [λατρεία], wherever it is placed in the holy Scriptures, our people interpret as servitude. But that servitude which is owed to men, according to which the Apostle commands servants to be subject to their masters, is usually named in Greek by another name. Douleia [δουλεία], however, according to the custom of those who composed the divine oracles for us, is either always, or so frequently that it is almost always, the name of that servitude which pertains to the worship of God. Therefore, if worship alone is said (namely in general), it does not seem to be due to God alone. For we are said also to worship men whom we frequent with honourable remembrance or presence; and not only those to whom we subject ourselves with religious humility, but some things also which are subject to us are said to be worshipped. For from this word come agricola, coloni and incolae. And afterwards: Because the word cultus is also used of other things, therefore the worship due to God cannot be signified in Latin by one word.

units.la: Similem ambiguitate ostendit esse etiam in vocabulis religionis & pietatis: Et a generali eorum significatione discernendas esse ...
units.tr: He shows that there is a similar ambiguity in the words religion and piety as well, and that they must be distinguished from their general meaning...

units.la: Ephes. 4. Coloss. 4. ait voces θρησκείας ac θεοσεβείας, non aliter, quàm vox λατρείας à generali voce cultus & servitutis discernenda fit. Hæc postquam cap. 1. de vsu horum vocabulorum disseruit Augustinus (cfi Ludovicus Vives in commentariis suis λατρείαν & δουλείαν idem esse ex Suida & Valla, & utrumq; significare seruitute ostendit) diserte capp. feqq.scribit: & illis immortalibus, ac beatis videlicet Angelis & nobis mortalibus, ac miseris, ut immortales ac beati esse possimus, unum Deum Deorum colendum esse, qui & noster fit, & illorum. Huic nos, inquit, seruitute, quæ λατρεία Græcè dicitur, fiue in quibuscunq; Sacramentis, fiue in nobis ipsis, debemus. Hujus enim templum simul omnes, singulí templa fumus. Quod postquam variis exemplis declaravit, sacrificiorum mentionem ingressus, cùm dixisset, Sacrificium nullus hominum est, qui audeat dicere deberi, nisi foli Deo: Mox quid per sacrificia illa V.T. significatum fit, ostensurus, inter alia ex Pfal. 51. citat dictum hoc: Sacrificium Deo Spiritus contritus, cor contritum & humiliatum non despicies Deus. Et ex Pfalm. 50. Immola Deo sacrificium laudis, & redde altissimo vota tua: & invoca me in die tribulationis, & eximam te, & glorificabis me.
units.tr: In Ephesians 4 and Colossians 4 he says that the words threskeia [θρησκείας] and theosebeia [θεοσεβείας] must be distinguished from the general word cultus and from servitude in the same way that the word latreia [λατρείας] is. After Augustine discusses the use of these words in chapter 1, he writes plainly in the following chapters (Ludovicus Vives, in his commentaries, shows from Suidas and Valla that latreia and douleia are the same and both signify servitude): "And to those immortal and blessed beings, that is, the angels, and to us mortals and wretched, so that we may become immortal and blessed, one God of gods is to be worshipped, who becomes both ours and theirs. To him, he says, we owe that servitude which in Greek is called latreia, whether in any sacraments or in ourselves. For all of us together are his temple, and each of us is a temple." After he has illustrated this with various examples, he comes to the mention of sacrifices and says: "There is no one among men who would dare to say that sacrifice is owed to anyone except God alone." Then, about to show what those Old Testament sacrifices signified, he cites among other things this saying from Psalm 51: "The sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise." And from Psalm 50: "Offer to God the sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High; and call upon me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me."

units.la: Sic igitur aperte Augustinus invocationem & gratiarum actionem cultum λατρείας nominat.
units.tr: Thus Augustine plainly calls invocation and thanksgiving the worship of latreia.

units.la: cap.յ. Hic locus est.
units.tr: Chapter 9. Here is the place.

units.la: Quid ? quòd cap. 14. prolixè disserit, an num Deum colendum esse (scilicet cultu λα-τρείας) non solum propter aterna, sed etiam pro-pter temporalia beneficia : nimirum ut ab illius cultu etiam in ipsorum desiderio anima humana non recedat.
units.tr: Moreover, in chapter 14 he discusses at length whether God is to be worshipped (namely with the worship of latreia) not only for eternal but also for temporal benefits, so that the human soul may not withdraw from his worship even in its desire for these things.

units.la: Postremò antithesin eandem ponit, qua & contra Faustum usus est : Putaverunt quidam, deferendum angelis honorem vel adoran-do vel sacrificando, qui debetur Deo, & eorum sunt admonitione prohibiti, justique sunt hac ei deferre, cui uni fas esse noverant. Imitati sunt angelos sanctos, etiam sancti homines Dei. &c. Hinc igitur luce meridiana clarius est, nihil aliud quàm fucum esse, cùm Jesuitæ prætex-tu distinctionis vocabulorum λατρείας & δου-λείας invocationem sanctorum stabilire co-nantur : cùm invocatio, utpote cultus soli Deo debitus, ad λατρείαν referatur ab Augustino, nec sine Idololatriæ crimine ulli creaturæ tribui possit.
units.tr: Finally, he sets down the same antithesis that he also used against Faustus: "Some have thought that the honour which is owed to God should be paid to angels, whether by adoring or by sacrificing, and they have been forbidden by the admonition of the angels; and they are righteous in not offering this to anyone except the one whom they knew alone to be lawful. The holy angels were imitated also by holy men of God, etc." Hence it is clearer than midday light that it is nothing but a pretence when the Jesuits, under the pretext of distinguishing the words latreia and douleia, try to establish the invocation of saints. For invocation, as worship due to God alone, is referred by Augustine to latreia, and it cannot be ascribed to any creature without the crime of idolatry.

units.la: Quid verò ad reliquas Jesuitarum objectiones in Catechismo Austriaco respondes?
units.tr: What do you reply to the remaining objections of the Jesuits in the Austrian Catechism?

units.la: Pergit Catechismus Austriacus tenebras manifestæ luci offundere: &c, quod sanctos in hunc modum (scilicet non cultu λατρείας, sed δουλείας) invocamus: adeo, inquit, Christi Salvatoris & Domini nostri gloriam non obscurat,
units.tr: The Austrian Catechism goes on to pour darkness over manifest light, saying: "that we invoke the saints in this way (namely not with the worship of latreia but of douleia); so far from obscuring, it says, the glory of Christ our Saviour and Lord,"

units.la: Christi gloriam amplificari ex Sanctorum cultu δου-λείας. ut etiam magis ac magis illustret, amplificet, augeatque.
units.tr: "the glory of Christ is increased by the worship of douleia to the saints, so that it shines more and more, is enlarged and grows."

units.la: Respon. Haec vero protestatio est, ut loquuntur, contraria facto. Nam quicquid Sanctis tribuitur ex iis, quae uni Christo debentur,id Christo ipsi detrahitur: sicut supra ostensum est, inter argumenta, quibus confirmatur Deitas Christi, hoc esse non postremum, quod Prophetae & Apostoli jubent invocari Christum. Hoc vero argumentum non solum obscuratur, sed etiam labefactatur, si angelis aut hominibus invocatio tribuenda est.
units.tr: The answer: this protestation is, as they say, contrary to the fact. For whatever is given to the saints of those things that are owed to Christ alone is taken away from Christ himself. As was shown above, among the arguments by which the deity of Christ is confirmed, this is not the least: that the prophets and apostles command Christ to be invoked. But this argument is not only obscured but even weakened if invocation is to be ascribed to angels or to men.

units.la: Deinde aliquoties dictum est, Mediatoris officium soli Christo congruere, & propitiationis sive meritorum, & intercessionis sive deprecationis respectu. Hic honos Christo adimitur, cum invocatur sancti, ut meritis & suffragiis suis apud Deum pro nobis intercedant.
units.tr: Then it has been said several times that the office of Mediator belongs to Christ alone, both with respect to propitiation or merits and with respect to intercession or entreaty. This honour is taken from Christ when the saints are invoked, that they may intercede for us with God by their merits and suffrages.

units.la: Praeterea, si non tantum de Christo, sed de Dei gloria in genere loquamur: scriptum est, Esa. 42. Ego Dominus, hoc est nomen meum, gloriam meam non dabo alii. Est autem invocatio gloria Dei propriissima. Itaque cum ad creaturas transfertur, imminuitur gloria Deo debita, & mera idololatria committitur, quantumcunque per cultum λατρείας excusetur. Res enim ipsa spectanda est, non fucus vocabulorum: neque rei prorsus incommunicabilis, modiaut gradus communicationis diversç pro nostro arbitrio fingen* disunt.
units.tr: Moreover, if we speak not only of Christ but of the glory of God in general, it is written in Isaiah 42: "I am the Lord; this is my name; I will not give my glory to another." Now invocation is most properly the glory of God. Therefore, when it is transferred to creatures, the glory due to God is diminished, and pure idolatry is committed, however much it is excused by the worship of latreia. For the thing itself must be regarded, not the pretence of words; nor may degrees or modes of a communication of what is wholly incommunicable be invented at our discretion.

units.la: Nam ut maritus rivalem in amore conjugali non potest ferre, neque excusationem uxoris adulteræ admitteret, affirmantis, se summo amore maritum prosequi, inferiori autem gradu amare adulterum: Sic Deus Optimus Maximus Zelotem se nominat, & se unum tota mente, tota anima, toto corde, toto inquam, non diviso aut dimidiato, diligi præcipit: neque hic, ut est in versu Potæ,
units.tr: For just as a husband cannot bear a rival in conjugal love, nor would he admit the excuse of an adulterous wife who affirms that she loves her husband with the greatest love, but loves the adulterer with a lesser degree: so God, Most Good and Greatest, names himself Jealous, and commands that he alone be loved with the whole mind, the whole soul, the whole heart; the whole, I say, not divided or halved. Nor is it the case here, as in the verse of the poet,

units.la: Divisum imperium cum Iove Cæsar habet. hoc est, nequaquam Sancti cultum invocationis divisum habent cum Deo, de quo uno distichon hoc αἰνιγμαλῶδες rectè factum est:
units.tr: "Caesar holds the empire divided with Jove": that is, the saints by no means hold the worship of invocation divided with God. Concerning him alone this distich, riddling in form, has been rightly composed:

units.la: Dimidium lunæ: tum solem : tum canis iram, Postulat à nobis conditor ipse Deus.
units.tr: "Half of the moon, then the sun, then the dog's rage: the Creator God himself demands these from us."

units.la: ALIUD JESUITARUM SO-phisma.
units.tr: ANOTHER SOPHISM OF THE JESUITS.

units.la: Atqui, inquit Catechesis, eximia Christi redemptoris virtus hic splendescit ac gloria, quod is non quidem in se tantum; sed in Sanctis etiam suis est, apparetq; potens, gloriosus, mirabilis: Quod eosdem honorat ipse, nimisque honorari vult in cœlo & in terra: quod per hos itidem, & propter hos multa largitur, & parcit sæpe immerentibus, ventibus, ut in Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, David, Jeremia cernimus, qui etiam defuncti vivi profuisse leguntur.
units.tr: "But," says the Catechism, "the outstanding virtue of Christ the Redeemer shines and is glorified here, in that he is not only in himself but is also in his Saints, and appears powerful, glorious and wonderful. He honours them himself and wishes to be greatly honoured in heaven and on earth. Through them, and for their sake, he bestows many gifts and often spares the undeserving, as we see in Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, David and Jeremiah, who are read to have helped others even after their deaths."

units.la: Respondeo primùm per inversionem.Christus in Sanctis suis potens, gloriosus, mirabilis est: Non igitur Sancti ipsi, sive vivi, sive mortui sint; sed Christus, cui virtus & gloria omnis tribuenda est, juxta illud Apostoli Galat. 1. Glorificabant in me Deum.
units.tr: I answer first by inversion. Christ is powerful, glorious and wonderful in his Saints. Therefore it is not the Saints themselves, whether living or dead, but Christ to whom all virtue and glory must be ascribed, according to the Apostle's words in Gal. 1: "They glorified God in me."

units.la: Potest & per instantiam responderi. Apparent mundani Principes in suis ministris potentes ac gloriosi, sed non propterea a ministris petendum est, quod unus ac solus Princeps praestare & vult & potest.
units.tr: It can also be answered by instance. Worldly princes appear powerful and glorious in their ministers, yet it does not follow that one must ask the ministers for favours, since one sole Prince both wills and is able to grant them.

units.la: Quod verò ex postremo versu Psalmi citatur, qui secundum vulgatam editionem est 67. cùm sit in hebraeo 68, Mirabilis Deus in Sanctis suis: id proprie pertinet ad praesentiam & efficaciam Dei in Ecclesia adhuc militante, ut praecedentia & sequentia demonstrant: Dabit voci suae vocem virtutis: super Israel magnificentia ejus. Item: Deus Israel ipse dabit virtutem & fortitudinem plebi suae.
units.tr: As for the last verse of the Psalm cited, which is Psalm 67 in the Vulgate edition but 68 in the Hebrew, "God is wonderful in his Saints": this properly pertains to the presence and efficacy of God in the Church still militant, as the preceding and following verses show: "He will give to his voice a voice of power; his majesty is over Israel." Likewise: "The God of Israel himself will give power and strength to his people."

units.la: Secundo, quod de honore Sanctorum apud Deum dicitur ex verbis Christi Joh. 12. Si quis servierit mihi, eum honorabit Pater meus: id quidem ad remunerationem pietatis in fidelibus, in hac & futura vita pertinet, &c.
units.tr: Secondly, what is said of the honour of the Saints before God, from the words of Christ in John 12: "If anyone serves me, my Father will honour him." This indeed pertains to the reward of piety in the faithful, in this life and in the life to come, etc.

units.la: &c. & cum illo convenit,quod olim per Prophe-tam Dominus dixit, Honorantes me honora-bo. Quod fit, cùm etiam in hoc seculo glo-ria& honore coronantur,qui in periculis glo-ria m Christi constanter defenderunt.
units.tr: Etc. And it agrees with what the Lord once said through the Prophet: "Those who honour me I will honour." This happens when, even in this age, those who constantly defended the glory of Christ in dangers are crowned with glory and honour.

units.la: Deinde etiamsi omne genus contumeliæ sustineant in mundo, & morte insuper igno-miniosa sæpè è medio tollantur:memoriæ ta-men ipsorum consulit Deus, ut apud poste-ros in honore & precio sint, qui dum in vivis erant, omnium odiis & conviciis proscinde-bantur.
units.tr: Then, even if they endure every kind of insult in the world, and are often taken out of the midst of us by a shameful death, God nevertheless takes thought for their memory, so that among posterity they are held in honour and esteem, though while they were alive they were torn apart by the hatred and reproaches of all.

units.la: Præterea, quod ex Psalm. 138. qui He-bræis 139. est, citatur versus 16. Mihi autem nimis honorificati sunt amici tui, Deus, nimis confortatus est principatus eorum. Dinumerabo eos, & super arenam multiplicabuntur. Certum est, hæc verba Psalmi in fontibus nullâ prorsus mentionem facere sanctorum: sed hoc solùm dicere: Quàm preciosa mihi sunt cogitationes tuæ Deus? Quam fortes sunt summæ earum? Si numerum eas, præ arena multiplicabuntur.
units.tr: Further, the verse of Psalm 138 (139 in Hebrew) cited is verse 16: "But to me your friends are exceedingly honoured, O God; their principality is exceedingly strengthened. I will number them, and they will be multiplied above the sand." It is certain that these words of the Psalm, in the sources, make no mention of the saints at all, but say only: "How precious to me are your thoughts, O God! How great are their sums! If I count them, they will be multiplied beyond the sand."

units.la: Nam vocabulum Reah, etsi in hebræo nunc amicum, nunc familiarem cogitationem significat: tamen hoc loco ne potest quidem aliter, quàm de cogitationibus intelligi, ut mox initio Psalmi hujus v. 2. sic usurpatur: Intelligis cogitationem meam eminus; sive procul. et totus contextus Psalmi ostendit hoc di-ci: In formatione hominis, & totius vitæ hu-manæ mànæ gubernatione, tàm miranda consilia esse sapientiæ divinæ, ut tacitus ea potius expendat, & secum admiretur ipse quàm oratione compleƈti, aut recensere omnia audeat, utpote quæ molesua mentes humanas obruant, neque ullo numero comprehendi possint.
units.tr: For the word reah, though in Hebrew it sometimes means a friend and sometimes a familiar thought, here can only be understood of thoughts, as it is used at the beginning of this same Psalm, v. 2: "You understand my thought from afar." And the whole context of the Psalm shows that this is what is said: in the formation of man and the governance of the whole of human life, the counsels of divine wisdom are so wonderful that one weighs them in silence and marvels at them inwardly, rather than dares to comprehend them all in speech or recount them, since they overwhelm human minds and cannot be grasped by any number.

units.la: Sed quanquam versio 70. interpretum, quam secuta est vetus latina versio, contextui Psalmi non quadrat: Tamen sententia hæc, utcunq; tolerari potest: eos,quosChristus quoq; Joh. 15. non servos, sed amicos suos vocat, quiq; apud Dominum jam præsentes sunt, 2. Cor. 5. in magno apud nos precio habendos esse.
units.tr: But although the version of the Seventy, which the old Latin version followed, does not fit the context of the Psalm, nevertheless this sense can be tolerated in some way: that those whom Christ also, in John 15, calls not servants but friends, and who are already present with the Lord (2 Cor. 5), are to be held in great esteem by us.

units.la: Verùm neq; ex hoc, quòd honorari Deus vult Sanƈtos suos in cœlo & in terra, sequitur, quòd precatione, atque invocatione honorandi sint? Alii sunt enim honoris gradus, quibusSanƈtorum memoria conservanda est in Ecclesia, etiamsi non dirigatur ad eos invocatio. Agendæ sunt enim gratiæ Deo, quòd se patefecit Ecclesiæ, & certum doƈtrinæ genus tradidit per Prophetas & Apostolos, & quòd doƈtrinam propagavit per Martyres & alios, eximiis donis instruƈtos, quibus cùm illi rectè usi sint, ipsorum quoque diligentia laudanda est, quòd curarint, ne frustra Dei gratiam acceperint. Deinde doƈtrinæ testimonia consideranda sunt, quæ per illos Deus edidit, & exempla judicii & misericordiæ divinæ in ipsis exhibitæ, quibus & timor Dei excitandus, & fides nobis confirmanda est. Denique & virtutes eorum imitandæ sunt, pro modo vocationis, & petendum à Deo, ut nos quoq; similiter regat, & organa salutaria nobis atq; aliis efficiat. Sed de his gratdibus honoris sanctorum paulò ante quoq; dictum est, qui nequaquam eò extendi debent, ut invocatio ad sanctos facienda sit.
units.tr: But does it not follow from the fact that God wishes his Saints to be honoured in heaven and on earth that they must be honoured by prayer and invocation? There are different degrees of honour, by which the memory of the Saints is to be preserved in the Church, even if invocation is not directed to them. For thanks must be given to God, because he revealed himself to the Church and handed down a certain kind of doctrine through the Prophets and Apostles, and because he spread that doctrine through the Martyrs and others endowed with outstanding gifts. Since they used these gifts rightly, their diligence too is to be praised, in that they took care not to have received God's grace in vain. Then the testimonies of doctrine which God brought forth through them are to be considered, and the examples of divine judgement and mercy displayed in them, by which both the fear of God is to be stirred up and our faith confirmed. Finally, their virtues are to be imitated, according to the measure of each one's calling, and it is to be asked of God that he likewise guide us and make us, and others, instruments of salvation. But of these degrees of honour for the saints something was said a little earlier, and they by no means ought to be extended so far that invocation should be made to the saints.

units.la: Tertiò de sanctis in hac vita constat, quòd per eos, & propter eos multa Deus largiatur, & sæpenumero parcat aliis: ut propter Abrahæ intercessionem sanatur Abimelech: & ad Lothi petitionem aliquandiu differtur exitium oppidi Segor. Aliquoties etiam deprecatione Moysis pœnæ mitigantur populo Israël: Et Esaiæ ac Ezechiæ precibus defenditur Hierosolyma, casu Senacheribi exercitu. Eliæ quoq; & Elisæi precibus mortui excitantur. Sic aliorum fidelium precibus multa fiunt ad publicam Ecclesiæ utilitatem. Nec dubium est, pios singulos omnibus temporibus sibi & aliis impetrare à Deo, tum depulsionem aut mitigationem malorum, tum plurima bona privata & publica. Itaque preces mutuæ, quas alii p aliis fundimus, cognitis mutuò necessitatibus nostris, nunquam sunt intermittendæ: sicut Paulus etiam sæpè petit ab Ecclesiis, ut pro se Deum precentur.
units.tr: Thirdly, it is established concerning the saints in this life that through them, and for their sake, God bestows many things and very often spares others. Thus, for the intercession of Abraham, Abimelech is healed; and at Lot's petition the destruction of the town of Zoar is deferred for a while. Sometimes too, at Moses' prayer, the punishments of the people of Israel are mitigated; and by the prayers of Isaiah and Hezekiah Jerusalem is defended, Sennacherib's army falling. The dead are also raised at the prayers of Elijah and Elisha. So by the prayers of other faithful people many things are done for the common benefit of the Church. Nor is there any doubt that individual pious people at all times obtain from God, for themselves and for others, both the removal or mitigation of evils and many good things, private and public. Therefore mutual prayers, which we offer for one another, our mutual needs being known, are never to be discontinued, just as Paul too often asks the Churches to pray to God for him.

units.la: Verum
units.tr: But

units.la: Verùm alia prorsus ratio est petendi intercessionem sanctorum in hac vita, quàm eorum, qui jam terras has liquerunt. Qui si precandi nobis essent, oporteret quoque, ut nos audirent, & necessitates nostras, cognitas sibi haberent: quod disertè negant sacræ literæ, juxta illud Esaiæ 63. & 64.
units.tr: But the manner of seeking the intercession of the saints in this life is entirely different from that of seeking it from those who have already left these lands. For if they were to be prayed to by us, it would also be necessary that they hear us and have our needs known to them. The sacred letters plainly deny this, according to the saying of Isaiah 63 and 64.

units.la: RESPONSIO AD LOCA SCRIPTURÆ citata in Catechesi Austriaca.
units.tr: Reply to the passages of Scripture cited in the Austrian Catechism.

units.la: Sed Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, David, Jeremias (inquit Austriaca Catechesis) etiam defuncti, vivis profuisse leguntur. Et allegantur in margine hæc loca: 1. Gen. 26. ubi promissio amplissima traditur Isaaco, eò quod obedierit Abraham voci Dei, & custodierit præcepta & mandata ejus, & cæremonias legesq; servarit.
units.tr: But Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, David, and Jeremiah (says the Austrian Catechism) are also read to have profited the living, even after death. And these passages are cited in the margin: (1) Gen. 26., where the most ample promise is given to Isaac, because Abraham obeyed the voice of God, and kept his precepts and commandments, and observed his ceremonies and laws.

units.la: 2. Exod. 32. Ubi Moyses deprecans pro populo, qui peccaverat vitulo aureo conflato, recordare, inquit, Domine, Abrahami & Isaaci, & Israëlis, servorum tuorum.
units.tr: (2) Exod. 32., where Moses, praying for the people who had sinned by casting the golden calf, says: Remember, Lord, Abraham and Isaac and Israel, your servants.

units.la: 3. 2. Reg. 19. Ubi Dominus per Prophetam consolatur Ezechiam, & defensionem urbi Hierosolymæ pollicetur contra Senna-cherib: Protegam urbem hanc, & salvabo eam propter me, & propter David servum meum.
units.tr: (3) 2 Kings 19., where the Lord, through the Prophet, comforts Hezekiah and promises the defence of the city of Jerusalem against Sennacherib: I will protect this city and save it, for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant.

units.la: 4. 2. Macchab. 15. Ubi somnium narratur à Juda Macchabæo, quòd Onias, qui summus Sacerdos fuerat, pro populo Judæorum ostantem viderit: postea & Jeremiam, qui non modò orârit pro populo, sed etiam 'extensâ dextrâ gladium aureum Judæ tradiderit, tanquam munus à Deo missum.
units.tr: (4) 2 Macc. 15., where a dream is related by Judas Maccabeus, that Onias, who had been high priest, appeared to him praying for the people of the Jews; and afterwards Jeremiah, who not only prayed for the people but also, stretching out his right hand, gave Judas a golden sword, as a gift sent from God.

units.la: Respondeo I. quod ad apparitionem Oniæ & Jeremiæ orantium pro populo attinet, Somnium id est Judæ Macchabæi, citatum ex libro Apocrypho, qui, inquit Augustinus, propter historiam utilis est, si sobriè legatur: non autem, ut testimonia indè ad confirmandam authoritatem fidei proferantur. Nam ad corroboranda ea, quæ in contentionem veniunt, libri Apocryphi semper minùs idonei habiti sunt in Ecclesia.
units.tr: I answer, first, as far as the appearance of Onias and Jeremiah praying for the people is concerned: that is a dream of Judas Maccabeus, cited from an Apocryphal book, which, as Augustine says, is useful for its history if read soberly, but not so that testimonies are drawn from it to confirm the authority of faith. For in the Church the Apocryphal books have always been regarded as less fit for confirming matters that are in dispute.

units.la: II. Nec tamen eo ipso in loco, vel Judas Macchabæus, vel milites, (ad quorum animos excitandos somnium illud recitavit Judas) sive Oniam sive Jeremiam, sed Dominum invocarunt. Quare etiamsi admittatur in hac disputatione locus ille ex Macchabæis: Tamen hoc tantùm sequeretur, Sanctos orare pro Ecclesia: Nequaquam verò invocandos propterea esse Sanctos ipsos.
units.tr: Second, in that very passage neither Judas Maccabeus nor the soldiers (whose spirits Judas roused by recounting that dream) invoked either Onias or Jeremiah, but the Lord. Therefore, even if that passage from the Maccabees is admitted into this dispute, it would follow only that the saints pray for the Church, and by no means that the saints themselves ought for that reason to be invoked.

units.la: Ad cætera verò loca, ex c. 26. Genes. & Exod. 32. Itemque 2. Reg. 19. Quibus & hæc sunt similia Genes. 32. in precatione Jacob ad Deum: Deus patris mei Abraham & Isaac erue me. Et Psalmo 132. Memento Domine David, & omnis afflictionis ejus. Vera & solida hæc est responsio: Quòd scriptura ipsa se declaret, quòd locutiones istiusmodi redi referendæ sint ad rationem fœderis, quo Abrahamo, Isaaco & Jacobo pepigerat Deus, se posteritati ipsorum benefacturum esse, & quòd Sancti in populo Dei sic orantes nitantur, non meritis majorum, sed promissionibus divinos ad patriarchas illos factis.
units.tr: As for the other passages, from Gen. 26., Exod. 32., and likewise 2 Kings 19., to which these similar passages may be added: Gen. 32., in Jacob's prayer to God, God of my father Abraham and Isaac, deliver me; and Psalm 132., Remember, Lord, David, and all his affliction. This is a true and solid answer: that Scripture itself makes clear that expressions of this kind must be referred to the covenant that God made with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, that he would do good to their posterity; and that the saints who pray in this way among the people of God rely not on the merits of their forefathers, but on the promises made by God to those patriarchs.

units.la: Sic enim Gen. 26. præcedit: Tibi & semini tuo dabo universas regiones hasce, ut compleam juramentum, quod spopondi Abraham patri tuo. Et Moyses Exod. 32. addit: Memento Abraham, Isaac, & Jacob, quibus jurastiper-temetipsum, dicens: multiplicabo semen eorum, et hanc terram dabo eis.
units.tr: For Gen. 26. goes before it thus: To you and your seed I will give all these regions, that I may fulfil the oath which I swore to Abraham your father. And Moses, Exod. 32., adds: Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, to whom you swore by yourself, saying: I will multiply their seed, and give them this land.

units.la: Sed & 1. Reg. 8. Salomon in dedicatione templi Psalmum 132. in hanc sententiam declarat: Nunc Domine Deus Israël, conserva famulo tuo David patri meo, quæ locutus es ei. Item: firmentur verba tua, quæ locutus es servo tuo David patri meo. Quò pertinet etiam, quod Psalmo 89. dicitur: Disposui pactum electo meo, juravi David servo meo: Si deliquerint filii ejus, non profanabo pactum meum: semel juravi in sanctitate mea, si mentiar David: ubi ergo sunt misericordiæ tuæ antiquæ, sicut juravisti David in veritate tua? Et 2. Paral. 21. Noluit Dominus disperdere domum David, propter pactum, quod iuerat cum eo.
units.tr: But also in 1 Kings 8., Solomon, at the dedication of the temple, declares Psalm 132. to this effect: Now, Lord God of Israel, keep for your servant David my father what you have spoken to him. Likewise: let your words be confirmed, which you spoke to your servant David my father. To this belongs also what is said in Psalm 89.: I have made a covenant with my chosen one, I have sworn to David my servant: If his sons forsake me, I will not profane my covenant; once I have sworn by my holiness, I will not lie to David: where then are your former mercies, as you swore to David in your truth? And 2 Chron. 21.: The Lord was unwilling to destroy the house of David, because of the covenant which he had made with him.

units.la: Etsi autem suo loco verum est, quòd Deus promiserit Sanctis propter pietatem præmia, atque inter hæc, quòd etiam posteris ipsorum beneficaturus sit: Tamen pii in suis ad Deum orationibus non merita patrum, sed contra iniam Dei promissionem allegant. Non enim dicunt: Exaudi nos, quoniam illi benemeriti sunt: sed quia tu promisisti: pepigisti, jurasti.
units.tr: Although it is true in its place that God promised rewards to the saints for their piety, and among these that he would also show kindness to their posterity, nevertheless the godly, in their prayers to God, do not plead the merits of the fathers, but rely upon God's promise. For they do not say: Hear us, because they deserved well; but: because you have promised, you have covenanted, you have sworn.

units.la: Sciunt enim pietati proposita esse præmia, non propter perfectionem operum, sed ex bonitate Dei gratuita, qui propter Christum, & personam & opus recipit, & præmia tribuit: non quòd opera remuneratione ista ex sese digna sint (cùm sint imperfecta & languida) sed ut divitias gratiæ suæ nobis ostendat, & coronet in nobis dona sua, ut Augustinus loquitur.
units.tr: For they know that rewards are set before piety not on account of the perfection of works, but from the free goodness of God, who for Christ's sake receives both person and work and bestows rewards; not because works are in themselves worthy of such recompense (since they are imperfect and feeble), but so that he may show us the riches of his grace and crown in us his own gifts, as Augustine says.

units.la: ALIVD SOPHISMA Jesuiticum.
units.tr: ANOTHER JESUITICAL SOPHISM.

units.la: Patres, quando de Sanctis loquuntur, nominant eos suffragatores, intercessores & patronos nostros.
units.tr: The Fathers, when they speak of the saints, call them our helpers, intercessors and patrons.

units.la: Ergo ex Patrum sententia Sancti sunt invocandi.
units.tr: Therefore, by the judgment of the Fathers, the saints are to be invoked.

units.la: Respon. In margine nuda nomina Basilii, Chrysostomi, Augustini, Ambrosii, Bernhardi annotantur: Sed neque loca, neque verba istorum scriptorum adscripta sunt, nisi quòd paulò ante Basilii concio de 40. martyribus citatur, & Chrysostomi homil. 41. in Genes. sicut & liber parvus Ambrosii de viduis. Et Eusebii liber 4. omissa mentione operis: & Hieronymi Epistola ad Riparium. De his ergo singulis ut respondeatur, loca ipsa authorum investiganda sunt.
units.tr: Answer: In the margin only the bare names of Basil, Chrysostom, Augustine, Ambrose and Bernard are noted. Neither the places nor the words of these writers are cited, except that shortly before, a sermon of Basil on the forty martyrs is cited, and Chrysostom's homily 41 on Genesis, as well as Ambrose's little book on widows, and the fourth book of Eusebius, with the title of the work omitted, and Jerome's letter to Riparius. To answer each of these, therefore, the places of the authors themselves must be examined.

units.la: DE LOCO BASILII.
units.tr: CONCERNING THE PASSAGE OF BASIL.

units.la: Ac primum in hom. Basilii in quadraginta Martyres haec leguntur: Martyrum memoria quasi satietas esse potest ei, qui martyres amore prosequitur? propterea quod honor, quem bonis conservis exhibemus, benevolentia erga communem Dominum significationem defe praebet, & eis, qui generosos viros amore complectitur, in similibus temporibus imitatione inferior non erit. Lauda ingenue eum, qui martyrium pertulit, quo fias martyr voluntate, & decedas citra persecutionem, citra ignem, citra flagella, eadem cum illo mercede dignus factus. Et postea: Hoc est martyrum encomium, exhortatio nimirum congregatorum ad virtutem.
units.tr: First, in Basil's homily on the forty martyrs, these words are read: "Can the memory of the martyrs become a satiety to one who loves the martyrs? Because the honour we show to good fellow-servants is a sign of goodwill towards our common Lord, and he who embraces with love those who were noble men will not be lacking in imitation when times are similar. Praise sincerely the one who endured martyrdom, so that you may become a martyr by your will, and depart without persecution, without fire, without scourges, and be made worthy of the same reward as he." And afterwards: "This is the praise of the martyrs, namely an exhortation of those gathered together to virtue."

units.la: Haec non ad invocationem, sed ad honorem martyrum pertinent, de cujus gradibus supra a nobis dictum est. Illa vero, quae sub finem attexuntur, duriora sunt. Hi sunt, qui nostram regionem Ἀγελαῖοι, id est, divisim capientes, veluti turres quaedam cohaerentes, securitatem ab hostium incursu exhibent: non uno loco seipsos concludentes, sed multis jam locis hospites facti, & multas patrias exornantes, &c., quod mirum est, non
units.tr: These things pertain not to invocation but to the honour of the martyrs, concerning whose degrees we have spoken above. But the things added near the end are harsher: "These are the ones who guard our region as Agelaioi [Ἀγελαῖοι], that is, taking it in separate parts, standing together like certain towers, they provide security from the attacks of enemies; not shutting themselves up in one place, but having become guests in many places now, and adorning many fatherlands, etc., which is wonderful, not"

units.la: D 4. fingilsigillatim diuisi ad suscipientes accedunt, fedinte r fe permixti unice tripudiant. Item: Quantum laborares, ut unum aliquem reperires, qui pro te Dominum exoraret? (Ϧυσωτηρ̈ν]α ὑπὲρ σῦ) Quadraginta jam sunt, concordem oreione sursum mittentes. Qui tribulatur, ad quadraginta confugit: qui latatur, ad ipsos decurrit. Ille, ut molestiarum solutionem reperiat: hic, ut res secunda ipsi conservantur. Hic mulier pi apro luberis orans deprehenditur, itemq; peregrin inti maritoͥ reditum, ac infirmo salutem petens. Er postea: O chorus sanctus, ô sacer ordo, ô confipatiu ac infractu agmen, ô communes generis humani custodes, ô boni curarum socii, orationum σωτῆργοι, legati potentissimi, stella terrarum orbis, Ecclesiarum flores, vos non terra occuluit! sed colum suscepit.
units.tr: ...(the text here is garbled in the scan) ...they approach those who receive them, each one separately, but mixed among themselves they only dance for joy. Again: "How much you would labour to find just one who would pray to the Lord for you" (who would intercede for you) [ὑπὲρ σοῦ]. "There are now forty, sending up their prayers with one accord. The one who is afflicted flees to the forty; the one who rejoices runs to them as well: the one to find release from troubles, the other that his good fortune may be preserved for him. Here a woman in labour is found praying, likewise a wife praying for the return of her travelling husband, and a sick man seeking health." And afterwards: "O holy chorus, O sacred order, O fellow-sufferers and unbroken army, O common guardians of the human race, O good companions of our cares, saviours of prayers [σωτῆργοι], most powerful envoys, star of the orb of the earth, flowers of the Churches, the earth did not hide you! but heaven received you."

units.la: Horum aliqua, etsi per Schemata Rhetorica excusari possunt, quibus orationes panegyricas, tanquam flosculis quibusdam exornarunt Basilius, Nyssenus, Nazianzenus: Tamen fateamur, quod res est: Jam tum illis temporibus in Ecclesia invaluisse opiniones de comprecationibus & auxiliis Sanctorum, qui sint veluti urbium custodes & locorum praesides, quorum interventu & precibus divina munera hominess consequantur. Consideretur autem praecipua quadam diligentia, Basilium, & qui cum eo consonant, in panegyres suas transtulisse comcompellationes istas Martyrum (quæ tamen ab ipsa illorum invocationedifferunt: non enim dicunt invocari martyres, sed hoc tantum exprimunt, quòd apudDeum illi pro nobis intercedant, & salutem àDeo afferant) non ex Scripturæ vel testimoniis, vel exemplis, imò nec ex veteris Ecclesiæ ritibus publicis, sed ex vulgi & mulierculârum privatis devotionibus, quas Monachi, qui circa illam ætatem ex Ægypto & Syria in Græciam propagati sunt, vehementer augebant, & confirmabant.
units.tr: Some of these, though they can be excused by rhetorical figures, with which Basil, Gregory of Nyssa and Gregory Nazianzen adorned their panegyric orations as with certain little flowers, nevertheless let us confess what is the case: already in those times opinions about the prayers and aid of the saints, who are as it were guardians of cities and presiding over places, through whose intercession and prayers men obtain divine gifts, had prevailed in the Church. Yet it should be noted with particular care that Basil, and those who agree with him, transferred these forms of address to the martyrs into their panegyrics (which, however, differ from the invocation itself: for they do not say that the martyrs are to be invoked, but only express this, that they intercede for us with God and bring salvation from God). These were not drawn from Scripture, either from its testimonies or its examples, nor indeed from the public rites of the ancient Church, but from the private devotions of the common people and of old women, which the monks, who in that age were spreading from Egypt and Syria into Greece, greatly increased and confirmed.

units.la: Cùm igitur citra verbum Dei & sine exemplo Scriptura, itemque citra morem primitivæ Ecclesiæ, panegyricè ista declamitet Basilius: nequaquam tanti facienda est in hac disputatione authoritas ejus, ut approbanda propterea sit invocatio Sanctorum, qualem Jesuitæ defendunt: quæ cum gloria perpetui regni & sacerdotii Christi pugnat, & falsam hanc persuasionem imperitorum animis offundit, quasi gubernationi Ecclesiæ Christus se abdicarit, & ministrationis suæ munera spiritibus defunctorum, qui ubique omnibus adsint, distribuerit.
units.tr: Since, therefore, Basil declaims these things panegyrically "without the Word of God and without example in Scripture, and likewise without the custom of the primitive Church," his authority must in no way be valued so highly in this dispute that the invocation of the saints, such as the Jesuits defend, should on that account be approved. That invocation fights against the glory of the perpetual kingdom and priesthood of Christ, and it pours into the minds of the unlearned this false persuasion, as if Christ had abdicated the government of the Church and distributed the offices of his ministry to the spirits of the dead, who are present to all everywhere.

units.la: DE LOCO CHRYSOSTOMI
units.tr: CONCERNING THE PASSAGE OF CHRYSOSTOM.

units.la: Chrysostomi homilia 41. in Genes. nihil prorsus habet, quod ad disputationem de Sanctorum invocatione, ullâ vel minima ex parte quadret. Sed homilia hanc sequente (scilicet 41. in Genes.) haec verba sunt: Virtus aliorum tegere valet multorum malitiam. Multa enim Domini bonitas, & saepe sole et etiam propter paucos multis dare salutem, & quid dico propter paucos iflos? Sape quando non inventus est in praesenti vita justus, propter defīctorum virtutem miseretur, & curam habet, unde clamat, dicens: Protegam civitatem hac propter me, & propter David servum meum: quasi diceret: Licet ipsi indigni sint, & nullam salutis habeant occasionem: tamen quia solitus sum misericorditer agere, & ad miserendum promptus sum, propter me ipsum faciam, & propter servum meum David, & qui ante annos e vita migravit, hic author erit salutis (sive incolumitatis) his qui sua sese perdiderunt desidia.
units.tr: Chrysostom's homily 41 on Genesis has absolutely nothing that agrees, even in the smallest part, with the dispute about the invocation of the saints. But in the homily following it (namely 41 on Genesis) these words occur: "The virtue of some is able to cover the wickedness of many. For the Lord's goodness is great, and often for the sake of a few he grants salvation to many; and why do I say for the sake of a few? Often, when no righteous man is found in the present life, he has mercy because of the virtue of those who have departed, and he takes care, whence he cries out, saying: I will protect this city for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David. As if he said: although they themselves are unworthy and have no occasion of salvation, yet because I am accustomed to act mercifully and am ready to show mercy, I will do it for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David; and he who passed from life years ago will be the author of salvation (or safety) to those who have ruined themselves by their sloth."

units.la: Verum haec eo saltem spectant, quod Deus facto ipso comprobare soleat id, quod ex gratuita bonitate promisit, ut misericordiam faciat in millia his, qui diligunt eum.
units.tr: But these words look at least to this: that God is accustomed to confirm by the deed itself what he has promised out of free goodness, namely that he will show mercy to thousands of those who love him.

units.la: Homilia vero 44. in Genes. non de precibus Sanctorum, qui sunt in altero seculo: sed de intercessionibus eorum, qui nobiscum in hoc seculo vivunt, agit, inquiens: Quando quod ex nobis est, simul afferimus (id est, conversionem ad Deum) & accedit intercessio Sanctorum, plurimum nobis confert. Quod si ipsi negligentes simus, & spem in illis solis collocamus nostrae salutis, nihil amplius nobis prodest: non
units.tr: Homily 44 on Genesis, however, deals not with the prayers of the saints who are in the next life but with the intercessions of those who live with us in this life, saying: When we bring what is from ourselves, namely conversion to God, and the intercession of the saints is added, it greatly benefits us. But if we ourselves are negligent and place our hope of salvation in them alone, it profits us nothing more: not

units.la: non quod infirmi sint justi, sed quia propter nostram desidiam nosipsos perdimus. Et postea: Id scientes confugiamus ad Sanctorum preces, & oremus, ut pro nobis intercedant: sed non illorum precibus tantum confidamus, sed & ipsi nostra, ut oportet, dispensemus recte, & ad meliora semper convertamur. Illud vero, quod sub finem ejusdem homiliae dicitur: Qui virtute praditi sunt, & castam vitam ducunt, non solum cum in hac vita sunt, sed & post vitae exitum, plurimum prodesse poterunt his, qui in se respexerint. No ad Sanctorum mortuorum intercessionem pertinet, sed ad exempla virtutum, ut haec verba praecedentia ostendunt: Bona opera agendo memoriam nostri relinquamus, ut cum hinc migraverimus, vita nostra diligens & accurata conversatio, sit monimentum & doctrina omnibus, qui in nos spectant.
units.tr: not because the just are weak, but because through our own sloth we destroy ourselves. And afterwards: Knowing this, let us take refuge in the prayers of the saints and pray that they intercede for us; but let us not rely on their prayers alone, but also, as we ought, manage our own affairs rightly and always turn to better things. But what is said near the end of the same homily: Those who are endowed with virtue and lead a chaste life, not only while they are in this life but also after their departure from it, will be able to benefit greatly those who look to themselves, does not pertain to the intercession of the dead saints but to examples of virtue, as the preceding words show: By doing good works let us leave behind a memory of ourselves, so that when we have departed hence, our diligent life and careful conduct may be a monument and a teaching to all who look upon us.

units.la: DE LOCO AMBROSII.
units.tr: On the passage of Ambrose.

units.la: De Ambrosii sententia ex libro de viduis idem respondeo, quod prius de Basilio: Non, ejus tantam esse authoritatem debere, ut quae contra scripturam sacram scripsit, imo quae alibi ipse refutavit, simpliciter, ut catholica, amplectamur.
units.tr: Concerning Ambrose's opinion from the book On Widows, I give the same answer as before about Basil: his authority ought not to be so great that we should simply embrace, as Catholic, what he wrote against Holy Scripture, or rather what he himself refuted elsewhere.

units.la: Videmus, inquit, quod magno peccato obnoxia minus idonea sit, qua pro se precatur: certe qua pro se impetret. Adhibeat igitur ad medicum alios precatores. Et mox: Obsecrandi sunt Angeli pro nobis, qui nobis ad praesidium datisunt: Martyres obsecrandi, quorum videmur nobis quoddam corporis pignore patrocinium vindicare. Possunt pro peccatis rogare nostris, qui proprio sanguine etiam, si qua habuerunt peccata, laverunt. Isti enim sunt Dei martyres, nostri praesules, speculatores vita, actuumque nostrorum. Non erubescamus, eos intercessores nostra infirmitatis adhibere, qui & ipsi infirmitatem corporis, etiam cum vincerent, cognoverunt.
units.tr: We see, he says, that one burdened with great sin is less fit to pray for herself; certainly not to obtain anything for herself. Let her therefore bring other intercessors to the physician. And soon after: The angels who have been given to us as our protection must be entreated for us; the martyrs must be entreated, whose patronage we seem to claim by a kind of pledge of their body. Those who have washed away with their own blood whatever sins they had may pray for our sins. For they are God's martyrs, our leaders, watchers over our life and our deeds. Let us not be ashamed to take as intercessors for our weakness those who themselves knew the weakness of the body, even when they conquered.

units.la: Haec quidem Ambrosius. sed ubi Scriptura docet, peccatorem poenitentem pro se orare non posse? cur vero non ad Christum, invitantem ad se omnes, qui onerati sunt, deducit? De quo in libro de Isaac & anima recte, & secundum scripturam idem ille Ambrosius inquit: Ipse Christus os nostrum est, per quod Patri loquimur: oculus noster, per que Patrem videmus: dextera nostra, per quam Patri nos afferimus: quo nisi intercedente, nec nobis, nec Sanctis omnibus, quidquam cum Deo est.
units.tr: These are Ambrose's words. But where does Scripture teach that a repentant sinner cannot pray for himself? And why does he not lead us to Christ, who invites all who are burdened to come to him? Concerning Christ, in the book On Isaac and the Soul, the same Ambrose rightly and in accordance with Scripture says: Christ himself is our mouth through which we speak to the Father; he is our eye through which we see the Father; he is our right hand through which we bring ourselves to the Father. Without his intercession, neither we nor all the saints have anything with God.

units.la: Cur Angelos obsecrare jubet, contra prohibitionem Angeli Apoc. 19. Cur martyres aliut peccata sua proprio sanguine lavisse? cum unius Jesu Christi Filii Dei sanguis emundet nos ab omni peccato.
units.tr: Why does he bid us entreat the angels, contrary to the prohibition of the angel in Apoc. 19.? Why does he say that the martyrs washed away their sins with their own blood, when the blood of the one Jesus Christ, the Son of God, cleanses us from every sin?

units.la: Cur ad hos detorquet, quod de solo Christo dictum est, Heb. 2. Quod ideo passus sit & tentatus tentatus, ut fieret fidelis & misericors Pontifex, & iis, qui tentantur, auxiliari posset.
units.tr: Why does he turn to these saints what was said of Christ alone, Heb. 2.: that he suffered and was tempted, so that he might become a faithful and merciful high priest and be able to help those who are tempted?

units.la: DE LOCO EVSEBII.
units.tr: ON THE PASSAGE OF EUSEBIUS.

units.la: Qui historiae Ecclesiasticae quartus liber est, nihil plane cum invocatione sanctorum commune habet: ac potius cap.15. hanc insignem sententiam in recitatione Epistolae Smyrnensium continet, qua prorsus evertitur Papistarum superstitio: Ignorant, nos nec Christum unquam relinquere, qui pro totius servandorum mundi salute passus est; nec alium quenquam colere posse. Nam hunc quidem tanquam filium Dei adoramus: martyres vero tanquam discipulos & imitatores Domini digne, propter insuperabilem in regem ipsorum ac praeceptorem benevolentiam, diligimus, quorum & nos consortes (scilicet in gloria) & discipulos (videlicet in pietate) fieri optamus.
units.tr: The fourth book of his Ecclesiastical History has nothing at all in common with the invocation of saints. Indeed, in chapter 15, in the recital of the letter of the Smyrnaeans, it contains this notable sentence, which utterly overthrows the superstition of the Papists: They do not know that we can never abandon Christ, who suffered for the salvation of the whole world of those who are being saved, nor can we worship anyone else. For we adore him indeed as the Son of God, but the martyrs we love worthily as disciples and imitators of the Lord, on account of their unsurpassable goodwill towards their King and Teacher; and we desire to become their partners (namely in glory) and their disciples (namely in piety).

units.la: DE HIERONYMI LOCO AD Riparium, tom.2. Epistolarum: Item de libro ejus ad Vigilantium.
units.tr: On Jerome's passage to Riparius (vol. 2 of the Epistles), and also on his book against Vigilantius.

units.la: Jam quod ad Hieronymi authoritatem in hac causa attinet, optandum erat, vel ipsius Vigilantii scriptum extare, unde de ejus sententia certo statui posset: vel Hieronymum non conviriis, sed scripturae argumentis causam eam egisse, de quo operae pretium est hanc Erasmi censuram considerare, cujus haec verba sunt: Ita in Vigilantium con-vitiis debacchatur Hieronymus, ut plusculum in eo modestia cogar desiderare. Utinam argumentis duntaxat egisset, & a convitiis temperasset. Ejusdem & haec verba sunt: Vigilantius natione Gallus, Barcillonensis Ecclesia, qua in Hispania est, presbyter, librum scripsit, in quo docebat, non esse, sic adorandas martyrum reliquias, nec ad horum sepulchra vigilandum, id quod id temporis magna religione fiebat a Christianis. Et postea: Vigilias nocturnas non placuisse viris Ecclesiasticis, vel illud satis arguit, quod horum authoritate sublata sunt, nomine duntaxat superstite, nec hodie simili studio concurritur ad martyrum reliquias. Haec Erasmus.
units.tr: As far as Jerome's authority in this matter is concerned, it would have been desirable either that Vigilantius's own writing survived, from which his opinion could be known with certainty, or that Jerome had argued the case with Scripture arguments rather than insults. On this point it is worth considering Erasmus's judgement, whose words are these: Jerome rages against Vigilantius with such abuse that I am compelled to miss a little restraint in him. Would that he had argued only with arguments and refrained from insults. The same Erasmus also writes: Vigilantius, a Gaul by birth, a presbyter of the Church of Barcelona, which is in Spain, wrote a book in which he taught that the relics of martyrs are not to be venerated in this way, nor is vigil to be kept at their tombs, which at that time was done with great devotion by Christians. And later: That the nocturnal vigils did not please churchmen is sufficiently shown by the fact that they were abolished by their authority, the name alone surviving; nor today is there such zeal in crowding to the relics of martyrs. Thus Erasmus.

units.la: Sed audiamus Hieronymum ipsum, qui in Epistola quidem ad Riparium stomachatur, Vigilantium (quem καλὰ ὑλίφρακτον Dormitantium nominat) contra Martyrum reliquias quaedam protulisse, & eos, qui illas suscipérent, cinerarios & idololatras appellasse, qui mortuorum hominum ossa venerentur.
units.tr: But let us hear Jerome himself, who in his letter to Riparius complains that Vigilantius (whom he calls Dormitantius [καλὰ ὑλίφρακτον]) had put forward certain things against the relics of martyrs, and had called those who received them cinerarians and idolaters, who venerate the bones of dead men.

units.la: Adeo autem Sanctorum adorationem non defendit Hieronymus, ut in eadem ad Riparium Epistola dicat: Nos, non dico Martyrum reliquias, sed ne solem quidem & lunam, non Angelos, non Archangelos, non Cherubim, non Seraphim, & omne nomen, quod nominatur in praesenti saeculo & in futuro, colimus & adoramus: ne serviamus creaturae potius quam quàm creatori, qui est benedictus in secula. Honoramus autem reliquias martyrum, ut eum, cuius sunt martyres, adoremus. Honoramus servos, ut honor servorum redundet ad Dominum, qui ait: Qui vos suscipit, me suscipit. In reliqua epistolæ parte tantùm hoc disputat: non esse immundas reliquias sanctorum.
units.tr: Jerome so far does not defend the worship of the saints that in the same letter to Riparius he says: We do not, I say, worship the relics of martyrs, nor even the sun and the moon, nor angels, nor archangels, nor cherubim, nor seraphim, nor any name that is named in this age or in the age to come, lest we serve the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed for ever. We honour the relics of martyrs so that we may worship him whose martyrs they are. We honour the servants so that the honour of the servants may pass on to the Lord, who says: He who receives you receives me. In the rest of the letter he argues only this: that the relics of the saints are not unclean.

units.la: In libro autem ipso contra Vigilantium tribuit ei, quòd negat martyrum sepulchra veneranda, & damnandas dicat esse vigilias, nunquam nisi in Pascha Alleluja canendum, contientiam hæresin, pudicitiam libidinis seminarium esse. Postea ex libro Vigilantii, quod ad Sanctos mortuos attinet, hæc loca citat: Quid necesse est, te tanto honore non solùm honorare, sed etiam adorare illud nescio quid, quod in modico vasculo transferendo coli? Et rursum: Quid pulverem linteamine circumdatum adorando ofculasimilis? Et prope ritum gentilium videmus sub pretextu religionis introductum in Ecclesiis, sole adhuc fulgente moles cereorum accenditur, & ubicunque pulvisculum nescio quod, in medico vasculo preciofo linteamine circumdatum osculantes adorant, magnum honorem præbent huiusmodi homines beatissimis martyribus, quos putant, de vilissimis cereolis illustrandos, quos agnus, qui est in medio throni, cum omni fulgore majestatis suæ illustrat.
units.tr: In the book itself against Vigilantius, however, he charges him with denying that the tombs of martyrs are to be venerated, and saying that vigils are to be condemned, that the Alleluia is never to be sung except at Easter, that continence is a heresy and chastity a seedbed of lust. Afterwards, from Vigilantius's book, as far as it concerns the dead saints, he cites these passages: Why is it necessary to honour with such great honour, not only to honour but even to adore, I know not what, which is venerated in the carrying about of a small vessel? And again: Why do you kiss and adore dust wrapped in linen? And we see almost the rite of the Gentiles introduced into the churches under the pretext of religion: while the sun is still shining, a mass of candles is lit, and wherever people kiss and adore some dust or other wrapped in a precious vessel and linen, such men pay great honour to the most blessed martyrs, whom they think must be illuminated by the cheapest little candles, whom the Lamb, who is in the midst of the throne, illuminates with all the splendour of his majesty.

units.la: Ad hæc respondens Hieronymus expressè iterum damnat adorationem Sanctorum.
units.tr: In reply to these things Jerome again expressly condemns the adoration of the saints.

units.la: Quis enim, inquit, o insanum caput, aliquando martyres adoravit? Quis hominem putavit Deum? Nonne Paulus & Barnabas, cum a Lycaonibus Jupiter & Mercurius putarentur, & eis vellent hostias immolare, sciderunt vestimenta sua, & se homines esse dixerunt? Quod & de Petro legimus, qui Cornelium se adorare cupiente manu sublevavit, & dixit; surge, nam & ego homo sum. Postea valde iracunde invehitur in Vigilantium, quasi ei hoc doluerit, martyrum reliquias pretioso operiri velamine, & non vel pannis, vel cilicio colligari, vel projici in sterquilinium. Et ironice quaerit, an sacrilegi sint, qui Apostolorum basilicas ingrediantur? an sacrilegus Constantinus, qui reliquias Andreae, Lucae & Timothei, transtulerit Constantinopolin? an Arcadius, qui ossa Samuelis de Judaea in Thraciam transtulerit? An Episcopi omnes non solum sacrilegi, sed fatui judicandi, qui rem vilissimam & cineres dissolutos in serico & vase aureo portaverint? an stulti omnium Ecclesiarum populi, qui occurrerint sanctis reliquiis, & tanta laetitia, quasi praesentem viventem Prophetam cernerent, susceperint, ut de Palaestina usque Chalcedonem jungerentur populorum examina, & in Christi laudem una voce resonarent. Sed & hic addit Hieronymus ironice: videlicet adorabant Samuelem, & non Christum, cujus Sacerdos, & Levita, & Propheta fuit. Quasi diceret: Imo nequaquam Samuelem, sed Christum adorabant.
units.tr: Who, you foolish head, ever worshipped martyrs? Who thought a man to be God? Did not Paul and Barnabas, when the Lycaonians thought them Jupiter and Mercury and wanted to sacrifice victims to them, tear their garments and say that they were men? And we read the same of Peter, who raised Cornelius with his hand when he wished to adore him, and said: Rise, for I too am a man. Afterwards he rails very angrily against Vigilantius, as if it grieved him that the relics of martyrs are covered with a precious veil, rather than bound in rags or sackcloth, or thrown onto a dunghill. And ironically he asks: Are those sacrilegious who enter the basilicas of the Apostles? Is Constantine sacrilegious, who transferred the relics of Andrew, Luke and Timothy to Constantinople? Is Arcadius, who transferred the bones of Samuel from Judaea into Thrace? Are all the bishops not only sacrilegious but to be judged foolish, who carried the vilest dust and dissolved ashes in silk and a golden vessel? Are the foolish peoples of all the churches, who met the holy relics and received them with such joy, as if they saw a living prophet present, sacrilegious, so that throngs of people were joined together from Palestine to Chalcedon and resounded with one voice in the praise of Christ? But here too Jerome adds ironically: Clearly they were adoring Samuel, and not Christ, whose priest and Levite and prophet he was. As if he were saying: Rather, not Samuel at all, but they were adoring Christ.

units.la: Secundò citat ex Vigilantii libro hæc verba: Ais vel in sinu Abrahæ, vel in loco refrigerii, vel subter aram Dei, animas Apostolorū & martyrum consedisse, nec posse suis tumulis, & ubi voluerint, adesse præsentes. Quibus ex verbis apparet, disputasse Vigilantium, animas beatorum non adesse suis sepulchris, nec interesse rebus viventium, qualis nunc temporis multorum fuit superstitiosa opinio.
units.tr: Secondly, he cites these words from Vigilantius's book: You say that either in the bosom of Abraham, or in a place of refreshment, or beneath the altar of God, the souls of the Apostles and martyrs have sat, and that they cannot be present at their tombs and wherever they wish. From these words it appears that Vigilantius argued that the souls of the blessed are not present at their tombs, nor concern themselves with the affairs of the living, which was then the superstitious opinion of many.

units.la: Quid vero ad hæc Hieronymum?
units.tr: What then does Jerome answer to these points?

units.la: Tu Deo leges ponis? tu Apostolis vincula injicies, ut usque adjudicii diem teneantur custodiâ? nec sint cum Domino suo, de quibus scriptum est, Sequuntur agnum quocunque vadit? Sic agnus ubiq̄: Ergo & hi qui cum agno sunt, ubique esse credendi sunt. Et cùm Diabolus & Dæmones toto vagentur in orbe, & celeritate nimiâ ubique præsentes sint: Martyres post effusionem sanguinis sui, ara operientur inclusi, & inde exire non poterunt?
units.tr: Do you lay down laws for God? Will you put chains on the Apostles, so that they are kept in custody until the day of judgment? Are they not with their Lord, of whom it is written, "They follow the Lamb wherever he goes"? The Lamb is everywhere; therefore those who are with the Lamb must be believed to be everywhere. And since the Devil and the demons wander through the whole world and are present everywhere with great speed, will the martyrs, after the shedding of their blood, be shut up and covered under the altar, and be unable to come out from there?

units.la: Hæc verò qualia, & quàm infirma argumenta sunt? Potest Deus facere, ut anima Sanctorum aliâs in cœlo sint, aliâs in terris: Ergò credendum est, animas martyrum esse ad sepulchra sua.
